b: Date saved: 2026-10-20 23:15 (PDT) Sources: Giffords Law Center, Colorado General Assembly, California State Senate, Washington State Legislature, New York State Senate Why it matters The legislative fight over who can use a 3D printer or CNC machine to make a gun has become one of the most active fronts in state-level gun policy, and the scope of what lawmakers are targeting has expanded significantly. The newest laws no longer just ban the printing of firearms — they now reach digital manufacturing code itself, the CNC milling machines that can produce firearm components, and even mandate that printers sold to consumers come with blocking technology baked in. New York became the first state to require blocking technology on all 3D printers sold, and California is actively considering a similar mandate. This matters because it is a direct collision between decentralized manufacturing and the state's monopoly on lethal force. The gun-control side argues that 3D-printed and CNC-milled firearms — "ghost guns" with no serial numbers, no background check, no paper trail — are a loophole large enough to drive a truck through. The counterargument, from the gun-rights side, is that attaching liability to code and machine tools fundamentally transforms a consumer device into a regulated instrument, with implications that extend well beyond firearms. The Colorado law's definition of "3-dimensional printing" to include both additive and subtractive manufacturing (which covers CNC mills and lathes) signals that lawmakers are thinking about the full toolkit of digital fabrication. What to watch next: whether the courts sustain New York's blocking-technology mandate when it takes effect (the law says "as soon as technologically feasible"), and whether federal action emerges — currently the federal government has largely left this to the states.
